body:
How newspapers contributed to the national movement

Newspapers were important instruments of political education during the freedom movement. They carried reports of government actions, explained nationalist demands, criticised injustice and encouraged readers to take part in organised public activity.

In Gujarat, nationalist journalism developed through publications connected with Mahatma Gandhi and through regional newspapers concerned with the affairs of Kathiawar's princely states. The distinction is important: some newspapers addressed the wider struggle against British rule, while others gave particular attention to the rights of people living under princes.

Navajivan: political education in Gujarati

Navajivan became a major Gujarati-language weekly under Gandhi's editorship. Its first issue in that form appeared on 7 September 1919.

The publication had an earlier history. Indulal Yagnik had been associated with the Gujarati periodical Navajivan ane Satya before its transfer and development under Gandhi. It would therefore be inaccurate to treat Gandhi as the originator of every earlier form of the publication.

Navajivan helped Gandhi communicate ideas about satyagraha, non-violence, swadeshi, social reform and public duty to a Gujarati-reading audience. Its importance lay not only in reporting events but also in explaining the principles and discipline expected of participants in political movements.

Young India: Gandhi's English-language journal

Young India was an English-language journal that Gandhi took over and edited in 1919. It already existed before his association with it. Its Ahmedabad publication under Gandhi's editorship is particularly associated with 8 October 1919.

Through Young India, Gandhi addressed readers across different parts of India, including people who did not read Gujarati. He explained political campaigns, criticised colonial policies and developed arguments concerning non-violence and national self-rule.

The use of separate Gujarati and English publications expanded the reach of related political ideas without making the 2 journals identical.

Saurashtra: a regional voice for princely-state subjects

The Gujarati weekly Saurashtra began publication in 1921 from Ranpur under the leadership of Amritlal Sheth. It circulated in Kathiawar and became associated with political criticism of princely administrations and the wider movement for public rights.

Ranpur was situated outside the jurisdiction of many of the princes whose governments the paper criticised. Publishing from such a location gave activists an important means of reaching readers in different princely states.

This newspaper illustrates why the press was significant to Praja Mandal politics. People divided among separate princely administrations could learn about grievances and movements elsewhere in Kathiawar.

The Harijan journals and constructive social reform

Gandhi's earlier major journals were followed by a group of publications beginning in 1933. These included Harijan in English, Harijan Bandhu in Gujarati and Harijan Sevak in Hindi.

These journals were closely associated with Gandhi's campaign against untouchability and with constructive social work. Their emphasis shows that nationalist journalism was not confined to demands for constitutional or political change. It also addressed social practices that Gandhi believed required reform.

Important newspaper distinctions

PublicationYear and languageKey associationPrincipal relevance
Navajivan1919; GujaratiMahatma Gandhi; earlier work of Indulal YagnikSatyagraha, swadeshi and public education
Young India1919; EnglishMahatma Gandhi as editorNational political arguments and mass movements
Saurashtra1921; GujaratiAmritlal Sheth; RanpurPrincely-state affairs and political rights in Kathiawar
Harijan1933; EnglishMahatma GandhiOpposition to untouchability and constructive reform
Harijan Bandhu1933; GujaratiGandhian publishing movementSocial reform for Gujarati readers
Harijan Sevak1933; HindiGandhian publishing movementSocial reform for Hindi readers

The newspapers differed in language, immediate audience and emphasis. Their roles should not be reduced to a single category merely because they were connected with the national movement.

Print and public mobilisation

A newspaper article could inform readers about a tax grievance, the arrest of a political worker or an appeal for reform. Readers could discuss the report in public meetings, circulate it among associations and decide whether to organise a petition, boycott or non-violent protest.

The process also worked in reverse. Political organisations supplied information to newspapers, which carried their demands beyond one town or princely state. The press and associations thus reinforced each other.

The historical use of a newspaper in a nationalist movement does not mean that every newspaper published in Gujarat was founded specifically for political agitation. Identify each publication by its documented history, language, associated individuals and principal role.

Prelims focus

  • Navajivan: Gujarati weekly under Gandhi's editorship from 7 September 1919.
  • Young India: English journal associated with Gandhi's editorship; Ahmedabad issue dated 8 October 1919.
  • Indulal Yagnik was associated with the earlier publication that preceded Gandhi's Navajivan.
  • Saurashtra: Gujarati weekly started at Ranpur in 1921 by Amritlal Sheth.
  • Harijan, Harijan Bandhu and Harijan Sevak began in 1933 in English, Gujarati and Hindi respectively.
  • Trap: Saurashtra was especially associated with Kathiawar's princely-state affairs; it should not be confused with Gandhi's Navajivan.

[Gandhi Heritage Portal, Journals by Gandhiji, Navajivan, Volume 1, Issue 1, 7 September 1919, and Young India, Volume 1, Issue 45, 8 October 1919, consulted 22 November 2026; Gandhi Heritage Portal, Chronology of Mahatma Gandhi, entries for September and October 1919, consulted 22 November 2026; Mahatma Gandhi, India Awakened, Volume V, account of Gandhi's journalistic work, mkgandhi.org, consulted 22 November 2026; People, Princes and Paramount Power: Society and Politics in the Indian Princely States, discussion of Amritlal Sheth, Ranpur and the Saurashtra weekly; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World – II, Class 10, Chapter 7, Print Culture and the Modern World, sections on print and public debate.]

pictures.alt: A press feedback loop turns grievances into mobilisation, while language journals and Saurashtra connect readers across princely states.
pictures.caption: Print helped connect information, political discussion and organised public participation.

title: The Nationalist Press in Gujarat: Navajivan, Young India, Saurashtra and Harijan

body:
Political associations as a link between leaders and the people

The national movement depended on more than prominent individuals. Public associations helped bring grievances to the attention of political leaders, organise meetings, circulate information and coordinate campaigns.

In Gujarat, such organisations operated in the directly administered areas of British India as well as in the princely states. Their work could overlap, but their immediate political circumstances were different.

Gujarat Sabha and political organisation in Ahmedabad

Gujarat Sabha was a public political association based in Ahmedabad. It provided an institutional setting for discussion of public grievances and political demands. Gandhi became its vice-president on 15 November 1915.

The association formed part of the developing political network through which Gandhi and his colleagues came into contact with people in Gujarat. Associations of this kind were especially useful because they could collect information from local communities and present demands through meetings, petitions and wider campaigns.

The Gujarat Sabha must be distinguished from a princely-state Praja Mandal. Its activity belonged primarily to the political environment of British-administered Gujarat, whereas Praja Mandals addressed the government of particular princely states.

The first Gujarat Political Conference

The First Gujarat Political Conference was held at Godhra on 3 November 1917, with Mahatma Gandhi presiding.

A political conference brought together participants from different places to discuss common public issues. Unlike a permanent institution such as a school or an ashram, it functioned primarily as a forum for political deliberation and coordination.

The date and location should be remembered separately from the Kathiawar Rajkiya Parishad's first meeting at Rajkot in 1921. The Godhra conference belonged to the wider Gujarat political movement; the Kathiawar organisation focused on the people of the princely-state region.

Ahmedabad's labour movement

The growth of textile mills made Ahmedabad an important centre of industrial labour. Workers faced questions concerning wages, working hours and treatment by employers. Public mobilisation therefore developed around labour rights as well as national political issues.

Anasuya Sarabhai played a pioneering role in organising Ahmedabad textile workers. Gandhi also became involved in industrial disputes. In 1918, he helped lead the Ahmedabad mill workers' satyagraha.

On 25 February 1920, Gandhi formally inaugurated a union of textile workers that developed into the Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association, popularly called Majoor Mahajan Sangh. Anasuya Sarabhai was central to its leadership, while Gandhi and Shankarlal Banker were associated with its development.

Majoor Mahajan Sangh: An organisation concerned principally with textile workers and industrial relations. Praja Mandal: An organisation concerned principally with political rights and responsible government in a princely state. Their activities were part of the wider nationalist period, but their immediate purposes differed.

Comparing Gujarat's important nationalist institutions

InstitutionPlaceHistorical associationMain function
Gujarat SabhaAhmedabadGandhi became vice-president in 1915Public political organisation
Gujarat Political ConferenceGodhraFirst conference in 1917; Gandhi presidedPolitical deliberation and coordination
Majoor Mahajan SanghAhmedabadAnasuya Sarabhai; development in 1920Textile workers' organisation
Gujarat VidyapithAhmedabadFounded by Gandhi in 1920Nationalist education
Kathiawar Rajkiya ParishadRajkot and wider KathiawarFirst meeting in 1921Political rights in princely states

How the different strands of mobilisation connected

Organisations worked through different sections of society. Political associations mobilised educated people and local communities; labour unions represented industrial workers; national schools and the ashram prepared students and volunteers; newspapers circulated political information; and Praja Mandals organised demands among princely-state subjects.

These were not separate histories without any connection. They shared political workers, methods of public discussion and the wider language of swaraj. Yet their names, founders, locations and functions remained distinct. Understanding these differences is essential for matching organisations with the correct facts.

Chronology of the main developments

YearDevelopment
1915Kochrab Ashram established; Gandhi became vice-president of Gujarat Sabha.
1917Ashram shifted to Sabarmati; First Gujarat Political Conference held at Godhra.
1918Ahmedabad mill workers' satyagraha.
1919Navajivan and Young India appeared under Gandhi's editorship in Ahmedabad.
1920Development of Majoor Mahajan Sangh; Gujarat Vidyapith established.
1921Kathiawar Rajkiya Parishad met at Rajkot; Saurashtra weekly began at Ranpur.
1923Rajkot's Praja Pratinidhi Sabha established under Lakhajiraj.
1927All-India States' Peoples' Conference established at Bombay.
1938–1939Major phase of the Rajkot Satyagraha.
1947–1949Junagadh accession dispute and administrative integration; formation of the United State of Saurashtra.

Prelims focus

  • Gandhi became vice-president of Gujarat Sabha on 15 November 1915.
  • The First Gujarat Political Conference was held at Godhra on 3 November 1917.
  • Ahmedabad mill workers' satyagraha took place in 1918.
  • Majoor Mahajan Sangh developed in 1920 with Anasuya Sarabhai as a central organiser.
  • Gujarat Vidyapith, founded in 1920, was an educational institution.
  • Kathiawar Rajkiya Parishad, first meeting in 1921, was a regional political organisation.
  • Trap: Gujarat Sabha, the Gujarat Political Conference and the Kathiawar Rajkiya Parishad should not be treated as alternative names for one organisation.

[Gandhi Heritage Portal, Chronology of Mahatma Gandhi, entries for 15 November 1915, 3 November 1917 and February–March 1918, consulted 22 November 2026; The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi, Volume 16, Speech at Gujarati Political Conference I, Godhra, 3 November 1917; Indian Labour Archives, Six Decades of Textile Labour Association, Ahmedabad, section Major Events, printed p. 5; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Heritage City, Majoor Mahajan Sangh, consulted 22 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 110–118; Gujarat Vidyapith, official Legacy and Objectives, consulted 22 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, Rajkot District, History of Rajkot, consulted 22 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Six connected strands show Gujarat's distinct political, labour, education, ashram, newspaper and princely-state contributions to the national movement.
pictures.caption: Gujarat's different institutions supported the freedom movement through distinct but connected functions.

title: Gujarat Sabha, Political Conferences and Labour Organisations in Public Mobilisation
